description:
BIG BANG THEORY

We don’t just think outside the box — we think outside the planet. A team of curious minds, bold ideas, and cosmic ambition, we’re turning real NASA data into innovative solutions for the Martian Map challenge. United by science and driven by curiosity, we’re ready to explore the unknown and push the boundaries of what’s possible.

Different minds. One universe. Infinite possibilities.
summary: Almost Astral is a layered, interactive map that helps the first astronauts on Mars plan and carry out a safe, science-rich Marswalk. We focused on the delta front of Jezero crater, Perseverance’s exploration site, and combined data from several NASA missions on one shared 5-metre grid: HiRISE imagery and terrain models (Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter), THEMIS thermal inertia (Mars Odyssey), CRISM mineral maps (MRO), space weather from NASA’s DONKI database, and a surface radiation estimate from Curiosity’s RAD instrument. From the terrain model we compute slope, roughness and cliff edges, and combine them with loose-sand indicators into a go / caution / no-go hazard map. Ground with no data is never treated as safe. A route planner uses this map to plan a walk from the rover to science stops chosen for their minerals, while showing the time back to the rover. Weather, radiation and solar storm data warn the crew when conditions change. The result is one view that answers the questions an explorer asks: where can I walk, what will I find, and how quickly can I get back?
details:
What it does. Almost Astral is an EVA (Marswalk) planning map for a crew landing at Jezero crater. It stacks several NASA data layers on one shared local grid (2000 × 2000 m, 5 m cells; coordinates in metres east and north of the site’s south-west corner), so every layer lines up exactly. Users switch layers on and off and change their opacity, and the map shows a north arrow, a scale bar, the coordinates and the hazard class under the cursor.

How it works.

  1. Terrain and hazards: from the HiRISE terrain model we compute slope, surface roughness (with the local slope removed), cliff edges and shaded relief. Together with THEMIS thermal inertia (low values mean loose sand), these produce a hazard map: go (below 15°), caution (15–25°, rough or loose ground) and no-go (above 25°, cliffs, very loose sand, plus a safety buffer). Cells with no terrain data are marked no-go and shown as “Unknown terrain coverage”, so the planner can never send a crew across ground we know nothing about. All thresholds are in one settings file so they can be tuned.
  2. Science: CRISM summary parameters flag olivine, Fe/Mg clays and carbonates, which are the minerals that make the Jezero delta a target in the search for signs of ancient habitability. Science stops are placed on these. [check: how your team chose the stops]
  3. Route and safety: a route planner finds a path from the rover through the science stops and back, avoiding no-go cells, and a “minutes back to rover” layer shows the walk-back time from anywhere on the map. [check with Tushaar: method, e.g. A on a cost map]*
  4. Conditions: space weather events (solar flares, CMEs, solar energetic particles) from NASA DONKI, a radiation dose estimate, and weather data feed alerts to the crew. [check: weather data source and how alerts are shown]
  5. Quality checks: automated tests and a validator confirm that every layer is on the same grid with the same georeferencing, and that the hazard map follows the agreed format. We also check that each layer lines up with the terrain model.

Benefits and impact. Astronauts get one integrated view instead of separate datasets, built around the questions that matter on an EVA: is it safe, what will I find, and can I get back in time? The same pipeline can be pointed at any Mars site that has a terrain model.

Honest limits. The radiation value is Curiosity’s average at Gale crater, applied unchanged at Jezero; Jezero is about 2 km higher, so the real dose is probably somewhat higher. Thermal inertia has 100 m pixels, much coarser than our 5 m grid. CRISM thresholds were tuned by eye.

Tools. Python (NumPy, SciPy, scikit-image, Matplotlib, Pillow, PyYAML, tifffile, rasterio) for the data processing; HTML, SVG and JavaScript for the map viewer; Git and GitHub for teamwork. [add your front end, e.g. React/Leaflet, if used]

Creativity. The hazard map treats missing data as a hazard of its own, and the viewer and tools can switch from stand-in data to real NASA data with one command.
